clinicalPearls: A rare histiocytic proliferation whose lesional cells share the immunophenotype of Langerhans cells (CD1a positive) yet lack langerin (CD207) and Birbeck granules, placing them at an indeterminate position between Langerhans cells and dermal dendrocytes.
It usually presents in adults as solitary or multiple asymptomatic red-brown to yellowish papules, plaques or nodules on the trunk, limbs, face or neck.
The disease is most often confined to the skin, but mucosal, nodal and rare visceral involvement have been described.
Lesions may appear in crops and can persist, progress or occasionally regress spontaneously, so the course is variable.
Histology shows a dermal infiltrate of histiocytes that are CD1a and S100 positive but langerin negative, and electron microscopy characteristically lacks Birbeck granules.

An association with haematological malignancies, particularly myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms including chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia and low-grade B-cell lymphomas, has been reported and warrants haematological review.

Some cases harbour clonal kinase-pathway alterations, including translocations involving the ETV3-NCOA2 fusion and BRAF or other MAP kinase pathway mutations, supporting a neoplastic basis in a subset.
It should be distinguished from Langerhans cell histiocytosis, which is langerin positive with Birbeck granules, and from the CD1a-negative non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses.
reference.pathophysiology: Indeterminate cell histiocytosis is a proliferation of so-called indeterminate dendritic cells, which display a hybrid immunophenotype expressing the Langerhans cell markers CD1a and S100 but, crucially, lacking langerin (CD207) and the ultrastructural Birbeck granules that define mature Langerhans cells. These cells are thought to correspond to a precursor or transitional dendritic cell that has not fully differentiated along the Langerhans cell pathway, or to a dermal dendritic cell that has acquired CD1a expression. While historically regarded as reactive, the identification of clonal molecular alterations in a proportion of cases, including the ETV3-NCOA2 gene fusion and activating mutations of the MAP kinase pathway such as BRAF, indicates that at least some cases are genuinely neoplastic. The reported co-occurrence with myeloid and lymphoid malignancies further supports a clonal, potentially shared-progenitor relationship in a subset of patients.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous involvement by leukaemia or lymphoma
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with immunohistochemistry (CD1a, S100, langerin/CD207, CD68)
Electron microscopy to confirm absence of Birbeck granules where diagnosis is uncertain
Molecular testing for ETV3-NCOA2 fusion and BRAF / MAP kinase pathway mutations where available
Full blood count and blood film to screen for associated haematological malignancy
Bone marrow examination if a myeloid or lymphoid neoplasm is suspected
Serum protein electrophoresis and lactate dehydrogenase
Imaging to assess for nodal or visceral involvement in extensive disease
redFlags: Cytopenias, monocytosis or abnormal blood film suggesting an associated myeloid neoplasm
Lymphadenopathy, organomegaly or systemic symptoms suggesting nodal or visceral disease
Coexisting or subsequent diagnosis of leukaemia or lymphoma
Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss or night sweats
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is variable and depends on the extent of disease and any associated haematological malignancy; purely cutaneous disease may remain stable, progress or occasionally regress, whereas cases linked to leukaemia or lymphoma follow the course of the underlying neoplasm.
pitfalls: Misclassifying it as Langerhans cell histiocytosis on the basis of CD1a positivity without testing for langerin or Birbeck granules.
Failing to screen for an associated haematological malignancy at diagnosis and during follow-up.
Assuming a uniformly benign course given the variable and sometimes neoplastic behaviour.
Overlooking molecular testing that may guide targeted therapy in progressive disease.
Confusing it with the CD1a-negative non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses and thereby misdirecting management.
references: WHO Classification of Histiocytoses and revised histiocytosis classification (current)
